#### Barrier alignment, and three recoveries from one crash

**What is being answered.** What barrier alignment costs, and why half a checkpoint is wrong rather than stale.

`align()` measures the cost in records: source "a" is ready at index 1, "b" at 5, and the condition `i > barrierIndex(EVENTS[i].key)` collects the 2 records that overtook their own barrier.

`recover(hasState, offset)` then runs the same crash three ways: 45 correct, 68 double-counted, 22 with the prefix lost. The two failures are symmetric around the truth, which is the argument for atomicity. And `errorBound(k)` takes only `k` — the interval is the error bound.

The animation steps through the code, holding each line long enough to read the STACK (call frames and their locals) and the HEAP (allocated arrays and objects) as they are AT THAT MOMENT. Expand any step to study it on its own.

<img src="../diagrams/anim/ch07-recovery-memory/ch07-recovery-memory.svg" alt="Barrier alignment, and three recoveries from one crash, 4 steps showing stack and heap" width="980">

<details>
<summary><b>Step 1 of 4</b> — the stage waits for the LATEST barrier, and buffers meanwhile</summary>

<img src="../diagrams/anim/ch07-recovery-memory/frames/step-01.svg" alt="Step 1: the stage waits for the LATEST barrier, and buffers meanwhile" width="980">

`latest` is 5 — source "b"'s barrier — while source "a" was ready at 1. The condition `i > barrierIndex(EVENTS[i].key)` catches records that overtook their OWN barrier: ids 3, 4. They belong to the next checkpoint, so they are held, not applied.

</details>
<details>
<summary><b>Step 2 of 4</b> — the matching pair reaches the no-crash total</summary>

<img src="../diagrams/anim/ch07-recovery-memory/frames/step-02.svg" alt="Step 2: the matching pair reaches the no-crash total" width="980">

`total` = PREFIX_V (23) plus the 4 replayed events (22) = 45. That equation is the whole claim a checkpointing design makes: recovery indistinguishable from no failure.

</details>
<details>
<summary><b>Step 3 of 4</b> — and the two half-checkpoints fail in OPPOSITE directions</summary>

<img src="../diagrams/anim/ch07-recovery-memory/frames/step-03.svg" alt="Step 3: and the two half-checkpoints fail in OPPOSITE directions" width="980">

Read the two heap rows together: 68 DOUBLE COUNTED and 22 LOST THE PREFIX, against a truth of 45. State without the offset over-counts by 23; the offset without state under-counts by the same 23. A half-committed checkpoint is wrong, not stale.

</details>
<details>
<summary><b>Step 4 of 4</b> — so the checkpoint interval IS the at-least-once error bound</summary>

<img src="../diagrams/anim/ch07-recovery-memory/frames/step-04.svg" alt="Step 4: so the checkpoint interval IS the at-least-once error bound" width="980">

`errorBound` sums the v of the events since the last checkpoint and keeps the largest — 12 at k = 3. Note what it takes as its only argument: `k`. The interval chosen in the previous concept for I/O and recovery time also sets how wrong an at-least-once answer can be.

</details>
